sentences.text: This dinosaur possessed a parrot-like beak, long arms with large claws, and slender fingers.
Its pubic bones measured 422 millimeters in length and curved backward at the base.
Analysis of the inner ear revealed posterior and lateral canals showing an incipient division.
It grew to about 2.50 meters, making it significantly larger than its relative Chirostenotes pergracilis.
The holotype specimen ROM 43250 was discovered in 1923 within the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Charles Whitney Gilmore originally described this specimen in 1924.
Robert M. Sullivan, Steven E. Jasinski, and Mark P. A. van Tomme formally named the species Epichirostenotes curriei in 2011.
Evidence suggests this creature was covered in feathers and functioned as an omnivore.
It likely hunted small prey such as lizards and larger insects.
Initially, researchers believed its bones belonged to an ornithomimosaur from the family Ornithomimidae.
Hans-Dieter Sues re-described the remains in 1997, proving they belonged to the oviraptorosaurian group instead.
Sullivan and colleagues later established it as a new species in the family Caenagnathidae.
Epichirostenotes curriei lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, 69 million years ago during the Maastrichtian.
The genus existed from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
Sullivan and colleagues argue that significant differences between TMP 79.20.1 and ROM 43250 justify recognizing them as different species, despite similarities noted by Sues in 1997.
